# The HiLiftAeroML ladders {#sec-data-efficiency}

**On the wings, GeoTransolver and Transolver are more accurate than ISLA
on every rung measured at the reporting protocol of 200,000 cells:
GeoTransolver by 27 to 32% and Transolver by 21 to 27% on the 35-case,
4-geometry and fixed-angle rungs, and the sampling budget does not change
that: on the two rungs measured at both budgets the ratios agree within
0.01 and 0.04 (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.73 at 200,000 cells against 0.72 at
10,000 on the 35-case rung; 0.69 against 0.68 on the fixed-angle rung).**
The ladders below train every architecture on nested subsets of
HiLiftAeroML and on two further ladders that vary what the training set
contains rather than how large it is, and score them all on the same
validation cases with the same instrument. The ordering never changes.
What the rungs add beyond the ordering is what ISLA's error responds to on
this dataset: it is paid in distinct geometries rather than cases (the
4-geometry rung costs ISLA 1.8x the 35-case rung at a similar case count),
and the deficit is not a shortage of sampled cells. The chapter also
carries the one wing result in which ISLA leads by a factor: trained under
a different sampling law, GeoTransolver and Transolver are 2.4 to 2.6x
worse on the 35-case rung and ISLA moves 1% (@sec-de-training-law).

Two conventions hold throughout, as everywhere in the book: the metric is
the area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure in float32 (@sec-metrics),
and a ratio between architectures is baseline error divided by ISLA error,
so a value above one would favor ISLA.

```{python}
#| label: setup-de
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
```

## What was measured {#sec-de-setup}

HiLiftAeroML (@sec-datasets) holds 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing
geometries, each simulated at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°. Three
ladders are used here.

- **The case ladder.** Nested random draws of 35, 210, 510 and 1,260
  training cases from a 1,260-case pool, sharing one 180-case validation set
  (@sec-splits). The validation geometries recur in training at other
  angles. The 35-case draw contains 33 distinct geometries and no case at
  18°.
- **The geometry ladder.** 40 cases on 4 geometries and 210 cases on 21
  geometries, each at all ten angles, validated on 180 cases of 18
  geometries that appear in no training set.
- **The fixed-angle split.** 126 geometries at 12°, validated on 18 held-out
  geometries at the same angle.

Every architecture trains under the frozen protocol (@sec-protocol) at the
reporting protocol: 200,000 sampled surface cells per case, 500 epochs,
bfloat16, no augmentation, two seeds, the freestream as a unit direction,
and each architecture at its own best learning rate (ISLA 1e-3, Transolver
3e-3, GeoTransolver the better of 1e-3 and 3e-3, which is 3e-3 on the wings;
@sec-lr-protocol). Every number is a float32 evaluation of the final-epoch
checkpoint; no checkpoint is selected on validation error. Parameters are
matched (ISLA 8.9M, GeoTransolver 9.0M, Transolver 6.0M) and so are tokens
per case; the step cost is in @sec-review-frontier. ISLA is the shipped
configuration (relative frame, @sec-isla); these lanes carry the
total-measure length unit, within 0.4% of the RMS-pairwise-distance default
at the reporting protocol (@sec-nb-lenrms-200k).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why every model receives the freestream as a unit direction"}
Fed the physical freestream velocity of 2,679.5 in/s instead, GeoTransolver's
global-context projector collapses to one occupied slice per head and both
baselines lose 3.4 to 3.8x at 35 cases. The mechanism, the control that
established it and the resulting protocol rule are in @sec-part-baseline;
every number in this chapter is a unit-direction number.
:::

## The ladder {#sec-de-result}

**GeoTransolver and Transolver are more accurate than ISLA on every rung
measured at the reporting protocol; the ratios are computed below from the
200,000-cell artifacts.**

```{python}
#| label: fig-hilift-data-efficiency
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The HiLiftAeroML rungs at the reporting protocol (200,000 cells per
#|   case). Surface-pressure error (area-weighted relative L2, float32) for
#|   GeoTransolver (red), Transolver (amber) and ISLA (blue) on the five
#|   rungs measured at this budget: 35 and 210 random training cases,
#|   validated on 180 cases whose geometries recur in training; 4 and 21
#|   training geometries at all their angles, validated on 180 cases of
#|   never-seen geometries; 126 geometries at a fixed 12°, validated on 18
#|   held-out geometries. Bars
#|   are seed means; dots are the two seeds; the label above each baseline
#|   bar is baseline ÷ ISLA. Panels share no vertical scale, since the
#|   rungs differ several-fold in error. How to read this: the baselines'
#|   lead is largest where the training set is small and its geometries recur
#|   in validation, shrinks with cases, and is within 5% where the validation
#|   geometries are never seen at 21 training geometries. It does not show
#|   the 510- and 1,260-case rungs, which are training at this budget
#|   (@sec-program-status), or the uncertainty from the choice of
#|   training draw, which is three to eleven times the seed spread at 35
#|   cases (@sec-de-controls). Data:
#|   results/p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-19.json (35 cases),
#|   results/p200k_fleet_interim_2026-09-20.json (4 geometries, fixed angle),
#|   results/p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-22.json (210 cases, 21 geometries).
#| code-fold: true
F19 = json.load(open(RES / "p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-19.json"))["datasets"]
F20 = json.load(open(RES / "p200k_fleet_interim_2026-09-20.json"))["datasets"]
F22 = json.load(open(RES / "p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-22.json"))["datasets"]
def gt_best(d):
    """GeoTransolver at the better of its 1e-3 and 3e-3 pairs, with the rate label."""
    a = d["arms"]; cands = {k: a[k] for k in ("gt_unit", "gt_unit_lr3e3") if k in a and a[k].get("n_evaluated")}
    k = min(cands, key=lambda k: cands[k]["pressure_l2_mean"])
    return cands[k], ("3e-3" if k.endswith("3e3") or len(cands) == 1 else "1e-3")
def rung(d):
    g, lab = gt_best(d)
    return {"gt": g["pressure_l2_seeds"], "gt_rate": lab, "t": d["arms"]["transolver_unit"]["pressure_l2_seeds"],
            "isla_ref": d["arms"]["isla"]["pressure_l2_seeds"]}
LADDER = {
 "35 cases": rung(F19["highlift_surface_super_scarce"]),
 "210 cases": rung(F22["highlift_surface_scarce"]),
 "4 geometries": rung(F20["highlift_surface_geometry_super_scarce"]),
 "21 geometries": rung(F22["highlift_surface_geometry_scarce"]),
 "fixed angle": rung(F20["highlift_surface_single_aoa_12"]),
}
PANELS = [("35 random training cases\n(geometries recur)", "35 cases"),
          ("210 random training cases\n(geometries recur)", "210 cases"),
          ("4 training geometries\n(never-seen geometries)", "4 geometries"),
          ("21 training geometries\n(never-seen geometries)", "21 geometries"),
          ("fixed angle 12°, 126 geometries\n(18 held-out geometries)", "fixed angle")]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(13.5, 4.6))
for ax, (title, name) in zip(axs, PANELS):
    r = LADDER[name]
    arms = [("Geo-\nTransolver", r["gt"], "gt"), ("Transolver", r["t"], "t"), ("ISLA", r["isla_ref"], "isla_ref")]
    means = [statistics.mean(v) for _, v, _ in arms]
    for x_, (_, v, k) in enumerate(arms):
        ax.bar(x_, means[x_], width=0.62, zorder=2, **bar_kwargs(k))
        ax.plot([x_] * len(v), v, marker="o", ms=4.5, mfc="white", mec=INK, mew=0.9, ls="none", zorder=4)
        lab = f"{means[x_]:.3f}" + ("" if k == "isla_ref" else f"\n÷ {means[x_] / means[2]:.2f}")
        ax.text(x_, means[x_] * 1.02, lab, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
    ax.set_xticks(range(3)); ax.set_xticklabels([a[0] for a in arms], fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9, pad=8); ax.set_ylim(0, max(means) * 1.3); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axs[0].set_ylabel("surface pressure error, area-weighted relative L2 [–]")
fig.suptitle("reporting protocol: 200,000 cells per case; label = baseline ÷ ISLA", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-ladder
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
def cell(v):
    m = statistics.mean(v)
    return f"{m:.4f} ({min(v):.4f}–{max(v):.4f})" if len(v) > 1 else f"{m:.4f}"
def ratio(a, b):
    return f"{statistics.mean(a) / statistics.mean(b):.2f}"
print("| rung | GeoTransolver (rate) | Transolver (3e-3) | ISLA (1e-3) | GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA | Transolver ÷ ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|")
for name in ("35 cases", "210 cases", "4 geometries", "21 geometries", "fixed angle"):
    r = LADDER[name]
    print(f"| {name} | {cell(r['gt'])} ({r['gt_rate']}) | {cell(r['t'])} | **{cell(r['isla_ref'])}** | "
          f"{ratio(r['gt'], r['isla_ref'])} | {ratio(r['t'], r['isla_ref'])} |")
print()
print(": The HiLiftAeroML ladders at the reporting protocol (200,000 cells per case) in float32: seed mean (seed range) of surface-pressure error on the shared validation cases, and each baseline's mean divided by ISLA's (below one means the baseline is more accurate). GeoTransolver at the better of its 1e-3 and 3e-3 pairs, the rate named per row; Transolver at 3e-3; ISLA at 1e-3. How to read this: the ordering, not the absolute level, is the result. Same sources as @fig-hilift-data-efficiency. {#tbl-hilift-ladder}")
```

**The deficit is a small-data, recurring-geometry effect.** Going from 35
to 210 random training cases shrinks GeoTransolver's lead from 27% to 11%
and Transolver's from 27% to 4%; holding the validation geometries out of
training, the lead at 21 training geometries is 2% for GeoTransolver and
5% for Transolver, against 24% and 27% at 4 geometries. Where a validation
wing's geometry recurs in the training set the baselines gain more than
ISLA does from having seen it, and where it does not the three models are
within seed noise of one another once the training set holds a few tens of
geometries. The 510- and 1,260-case rungs are training at the reporting
protocol and join the table as they report (@sec-program-status); the
preregistered bar for an ISLA advantage, baseline ÷ ISLA of at least 1.10
with ISLA lower on two thirds of the cases, is reached on no rung. The
orderings on velocity and wall shear follow pressure on every rung.

### The same rung under a different training law {#sec-de-training-law}

**On the 35-case rung at the reporting protocol, GeoTransolver and
Transolver trained under the area-proportional sampling law and scored on
the uniform draw are 2.6x and 2.4x worse than their uniform-trained twins;
ISLA is 1% better, so under the area-trained checkpoints GeoTransolver ÷
ISLA on the uniform draw is 1.9 and Transolver ÷ ISLA 1.8, against 0.73 and
0.73 for the uniform-trained pair.** The ladder above holds the sampling
law fixed at the training convention, uniform over cells; changing it is
the half of the discretization question a practitioner meets when a
surrogate trained on one mesher's output is handed a mesh from another, and
it is the one setting on the wings in which ISLA's lead is a factor rather
than a percentage. The figure, both datasets and the mechanism are in
@sec-training-law (@fig-training-law); the scoreboard row is
@tbl-scoreboard-training-law.

## Controls {#sec-de-controls}

**The two-seed spread at small rungs understates the uncertainty by a
factor of three to eleven; the training draw is the larger source, and the
ordering holds on every draw.** The 35-case split is one random draw from
the pool; re-running GeoTransolver, Transolver and the ISLA configuration
of the time (the legacy centered variant, removed; the interval measures
the draw, not the configuration) on three further geometry-stratified
35-case draws, three seeds each, puts GeoTransolver ÷ variant between 0.88
and 0.96 across draws and Transolver ÷ variant between 0.85 and 0.90, with
the curated draw typical for every arm; at 210 cases the same design gives
90% intervals of 0.82 to 0.93 and 0.85 to 0.95. Every 35-case ratio in the
book is to be read with a between-draw spread of this size. Data:
research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n35_fp32_2026-09-10.json
and campaign_a_n210_fp32_2026-09-10.json.

## What ISLA's error responds to {#sec-de-strata}

**ISLA's error is paid for in geometries, not cases.** Cutting the
training geometries eight-fold at a similar case count (4 geometries at ten
angles against 35 cases on 33 geometries) costs ISLA 1.8x at the reporting
protocol (@tbl-hilift-ladder). The comparison changes the validation
population as well as the training composition, so it supports a
geometry-count reading and not the stronger statement that geometry count
alone sets the error. Whether the deficit to GeoTransolver and Transolver
at the protocol width is capacity that ISLA recovers with depth, as it is
on DrivAerML (@sec-shared-floor), is what the wing scaling study measures
(@sec-program-status).

## Forces and an uncertainty signal {#sec-de-forces}

The integrated lift and drag coefficients of the validation cases, and the
two-seed disagreement as a ranking of per-case error, are evaluated on the
200,000-cell ISLA checkpoints as they report (@sec-program-status); neither
is a comparison, since GeoTransolver's and Transolver's forces and seed
signals are not reduced.

## What each ingredient costs ISLA {#sec-mechanism}

**No single ingredient is load-bearing for ISLA's accuracy, and the
measure weights are a correctness requirement whose in-distribution price
has a known mechanism.** Removing one ingredient at a time at 35 cases
(raw coordinates added as inputs, breaking exact equivariance; the
invariant seeds replaced by the raw vectors; a sample-estimated center and
length unit; the measure weights switched off; the relational invariants
removed from routing and read-back) gave one ordering: exactness of the
equivariance and the invariant seed set are not load-bearing in
distribution, an estimated center costs a few percent where validation
geometries recur and is inside seed noise at 435 cars
(@sec-nb-sgref-verdict), the weights-off ablation gains, and removing the
relational invariants is the largest single loss. The weights-off gain has
two parts: estimator variance, since with the weights on the effective
number of tokens per slice is about a fifth of the count, which shrinks
with cell count on the cars; and mesh-pattern content on the wings, where
the gain is flat in cell count and inverts under area-proportional
resampling, the weights-off error rising above that of predicting zero
while the weighted model's falls with count (@sec-consistency-bench). A
configuration that reads the mesher's cell placement is not a surrogate
for the surface (@sec-principle); the weights-off ISLA is an ablation and
never a configuration. The ablation was run on the removed legacy centered
variant at the exploration budget and is not re-measured, so no price is
quoted (results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-05.json).

## The same protocol on DrivAerML {#sec-de-drivaerml}

**On DrivAerML, GeoTransolver is the more data-efficient model by a
deficit that narrows monotonically from 17% at 27 cars to zero at 435,
and Transolver ÷ ISLA stays within 0.99 and 1.06 on every rung.** The five
rungs with seeds and rates are @tbl-scoreboard-200k and the anatomy of the
gap is @sec-deficit-anatomy; this is not an ISLA advantage but a deficit
that closes at the full training set.

## Limits of the claim {#sec-de-limits}

- **The ladder is a data-efficiency measurement, not a scaling law.** Its
  rungs span the range of data every production CFD dataset in this program
  occupies, and the curves flatten over it. On DrivAerML the flattening has
  a measured cause: every model's error is flat in the cell count above
  100,000, and given width and depth both architectures reach the same
  floor of about 0.040 (@sec-shared-floor). On the wings the scaling
  picture is being measured (@sec-program-status), so the wing flattening
  is not yet attributed.
- **It is in-distribution and a validation-set figure.** The validation
  cases share the training design; the checkpoints are final-epoch with no
  selection, but the validation set was reused adaptively for the baselines'
  per-rung learning rate and for what to present, and the sealed test was
  spent on regime extrapolation (@sec-limits-validation). Across a regime
  boundary no architecture generalizes (@sec-regime-extrapolation).
- **Seeds do not measure the choice of training cases.** The draw intervals
  of @sec-de-controls are the uncertainty to read, and they exist only at 35
  and 210 cases.
- **No mechanism of an in-distribution ISLA accuracy advantage is
  established, because no such advantage is established.** ISLA reaches
  parity with GeoTransolver at full DrivAerML data and trails it below
  (@sec-de-drivaerml); on the wings it trails at every rung under the
  training convention. What ISLA buys is stated with its scope in
  @sec-scoreboard: exact pose covariance (@sec-pose-contract), weak
  dependence on the training sampling law (@sec-de-training-law), a frame
  that converges under refinement (@sec-consistency-bench), the interior
  velocity lead on one dataset (@sec-interior) and the memory frontier at
  the scaling budget (@sec-shared-floor). The mechanism of the wing
  deficit, the mesher pattern where validation geometries recur in
  training, is the open study (@sec-open-questions).
